metadata.title: The Dual Role of Digital Self-Efficacy in Reading Engagement from a Nonlinear Dynamics Perspective

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade data from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, which is collected using a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design with probability-proportional-to-size (PPS) school sampling and class selection within schools. The PIRLS procedures include stratification and post-stratification calibration to align the sample with national population characteristics (e.g., school type, geographic region, urbanization, and socioeconomic status), implying that sampling weights are part of the official dataset. However, the manuscript does not report the specific PIRLS weight variable name(s) or whether the authors applied them in their cusp-model estimation. Because the analysis is conducted in R using the cusp package and the paper does not describe weight-aware estimation, the safest interpretation is that complex survey weights were not explicitly incorporated in the reported model fitting.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable (reading engagement) is derived from PIRLS questionnaire items using a 4-point scale and is not described as being imputed via PVs. The paper does report that reading achievement uses plausible values and that the first plausible value was used (with checks using other PVs), but it does not describe any missing-data handling strategy for the engagement/self-efficacy/liking scales or for the analytic sample after deletions (beyond deleting participants with fewer than two digital self-efficacy responses). This omission is a reporting gap because missingness in survey items can affect scale scores and model estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 4th-grade students from Saudi Arabia who participated in PIRLS 2021. The study uses the PIRLS 2021 cohort’s stratified two-stage cluster sampling design for representativeness. For measurement of digital self-efficacy, participants with fewer than two scores on the digital self-efficacy scale were deleted from the measurements. All model inputs (liking reading and digital self-efficacy) were z-scored before fitting the cusp catastrophe model.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 Reading (Saudi Arabia) — Reading engagement scale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Cusp vs linear comparison: AIC 8392.269 (cusp) vs 13,993.596 (linear); chi-square difference test χ2(2)=5605.000, p<0.001. Cusp model parameter tests (z-tests): liking reading slope a1=0.372 (SE=0.011, p<0.001); digital self-efficacy bifurcation slope b1=0.224 (SE=0.015, p<0.001); outcome slope w1=0.338 (SE=0.003, p<0.001). Multimodality test: Hartigan D=0.974, p<0.001; estimated six modes.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Grade 4 Reading (Saudi Arabia) the study leveraged liking reading and digital self-efficacy to predict reading engagement, finding that the cusp catastrophe model fit significantly better than a linear model and that digital self-efficacy shows a bifurcation pattern (linear-positive at low levels but chaotic/unpredictable engagement at higher levels). This indicates that digital self-efficacy interventions should be designed to avoid overconfidence effects at high efficacy levels and to support sustained, deep engagement rather than assuming uniformly increasing benefits.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PIRLS 2021 fourth-grade data from Saudi Arabia (N=4386) to model reading engagement as a nonlinear outcome using the cusp catastrophe model in R. Reading engagement is measured with nine PIRLS questionnaire items on a 4-point scale, and digital self-efficacy and liking reading are each measured via PIRLS scales; participants with fewer than two digital self-efficacy responses were deleted from measurement. The cusp model was strongly favored over a linear and logistic comparison using information criteria (AIC 8392.269 for cusp vs 13,993.596 for linear) and a nested-model chi-square difference test (χ2(2)=5605.000, p<0.001). The bifurcation term for digital self-efficacy was significant (b1=0.224, p<0.001), and the outcome distribution supported the cusp assumption of multimodality (Hartigan D=0.974, p<0.001; six modes). The paper does not report a missing-data strategy for engagement/self-efficacy items and does not specify whether PIRLS sampling weights were applied in the cusp estimation, limiting generalizability of effect magnitudes.
